cognate: Lithuanian žvaigždė and Serbian zvezda/zvijezda continue the same Balto-Slavic star noun; sesūtė and sestrica are diminutive formations on inherited sister vocabulary (*swesor-). The slab star reconstruction is a mapping label, not independent proof of a PIE star formation.
drift_or_renewal: Different productive diminutives; Lithuanian unspecified star versus Serbian travelling/morning star.
shared_syntax: Appositional star + sister, referring to the same celestial being; nominative Lithuanian, genitive or vocative Serbian.
context: The Lithuanian star acts as the bride’s sister, weaving her wreath; adjacent celestial father/brother roles place this in a heavenly family. Serbian Vuk 36196 places sister-star next to brother-moon; Vuk 35651 directly addresses the morning star as sister. The specific family role plus matching appositional nouns is more selective than merely naming a star. Both witnesses are late folklore: common Balto-Slavic inheritance is a defensible hypothesis, but later diffusion remains possible; these data alone do not establish pan-Indo-European antiquity.

cognate: imti ~ uzimati share *h1em-; ranka ~ ruka are cognate Balto-Slavic hand nouns; baltas ~ bijel continue related *bhel- white formations, not identical adjective suffixes.
drift_or_renewal: Negative Lithuanian taking with genitive of negation; affirmative Serbian taking with za + accusative. Diminutives in the second Lithuanian witness.
shared_syntax: Taking a woman’s white hand: TAKE governs a hand phrase whose epithet is WHITE, with cognate material in all three slots.
context: Lithuanian refusal to take an offered white hand is followed by violence; the Serbian hero takes the girl’s white hand and leads her home. Both use a conventional bodily gesture in the relations of man and woman. The negative Lithuanian wording presupposes the same expected gesture. The three-slot poetic collocation is stronger than simple shared vocabulary, though the gesture itself is ordinary. Late sources and possible regional diffusion prevent a confident inference of prehistoric inheritance.

cognate: Lithuanian (par-/at-)nešti and Serbian nositi continue the inherited carry root *h1nek- with different stem formations; ranka ~ ruka is the same Balto-Slavic hand noun.
drift_or_renewal: Lithuanian prefixed past carry/bring versus Serbian iterative present; one crow/raven versus two ravens. White modifies the Lithuanian hand; no matching white-hand epithet is claimed for Vuk 1566.
shared_syntax: Bird subject + carry/bring verb + severed HAND as direct object; a gold/gilded ring identifies or accompanies the hand in immediately adjacent text.
context: The black bird brings a white hand and gold ring in both Lithuanian variants. The Serbian ravens carry a warrior’s hand bearing a gilded ring and drop it into the mother’s lap. Matching verb-object wording within this unusual death-token scene is substantially more distinctive than generic carrying. This is a tentative inherited Baltic-Slavic narrative formula, not a secure PIE reconstruction: late ballad transmission or borrowing could account for the entire motif.

near_miss.why_not: Exact adjective/noun cognates, but the matchmaker is a deceitful persuader, whereas the AVP fragment does not establish that speech metaphor. Search also finds literal monstrous tongues in Sanskrit epic. No shared distinctive context demonstrated.

Only bundle 16 actually joins vesti to daughter in a marriage question. Other pivots lead a man, or lead a daughter to a dragon. Even the valid bridal instance follows ordinary lexical vesti = marry; no distinctive inherited phrase beyond this shared lexical sense is established.

Lithuanian prašyti + melsti/maldyti is a recurrent synonymous doublet. Old Russian has reversed moliti sja i prositi with peace as object, not bridal solicitation. Generic intensification and shared Balto-Slavic lexemes are insufficient here. Corpus tests verify Lithuanian recurrence but furnish no independent early matching specialized scene; the Vuk search hit has a betrothed girl praying, not this doublet.

Genuine dog/bark cognates with arrival settings; however a dog barking is an ordinary animal predicate. Hermes’ dogs do not bark, and the Lithuanian dog does. The Pisander partner merely names a dog; not a bark predicate. Search finds repeated Lithuanian lines without establishing distinctive shared formula structure.

Cognate tekėti/teći and celestial names, but Lithuanian requests sunset and moonrise separately; Serbian uses an enduring sun-and-moon formula meaning as long as they last. Search confirms the Serbian formula, not the same paired predication in the Lithuanian line. The lexical cosmic-motion metaphor alone is insufficient.

The Lithuanian moon bows to stars in a dream; Serbian moon rebukes the morning star, and another partner depicts an emblem on a flag. Shared celestial personification, not a matching predicate or relationship. Dream framing also leaves literary/folktale transmission open.

near_miss.lead: carry in white hands / white towel
near_miss.why_not: The retrieved Serbian partners carry a banner in hands or carry a white towel, whereas the Lithuanian direct object is a severed hand. No shared syntax for those pairs. A better in-slab partner was located in bundle 152 and used in the cross-bundle claim.
Old Russian hand is subject of a separate capture clause; it does not express the means of leading. Lithuanian by-the-hand leading is therefore not syntactically matched, despite the shared roots.

Both noun and verb cognate, but Lithuanian visitor stands at a girl’s door, while the saint’s reliquary stops in a doorway. Routine spatial predication; no distinctive shared situation or poetic elaboration.

Cognate head noun but Lithuanian kirsti and Serbian sjeći are different cut roots. The narrative act is common; dragon decapitation and human execution differ. No distinctive inherited wording demonstrated.
Lithuanian actual enchanted wolf runs out; Igor compares a fleeing man to a grey wolf. Cognate wolf/run words do not establish the same poetic figure.

Correct flow/water or flow/stream correspondences occur in some partners, but they describe the most ordinary behavior of water. Ritual purification, geographical listing, bridal river setting, and Igor’s silver streams do not supply a shared distinctive formula. AVŚ 3.31 asaran belongs to sṛ, not sru.
Lithuanian impossible errand asks for hay in winter and snow in summer; Russian records lack of winter snow. The snow/winter words do not share the same assertion or merism.

Lithuanian all-season greenery uses winter and summer; Vedic longevity blessing enumerates autumns, winters, springs, and Cato gives agricultural instructions. Seasonal lexical cognacy does not establish the same formula or context.

near_miss.lead: fire burns stone / burn with fire
near_miss.why_not: Lithuanian cumulative tale has fire as agent and stone as object; Atharvan charm uses fire instrumentally to burn a worm’s face and stone to break its head. The recurrence of three roots masks different syntactic groupings.

Genuine cognate north/wind collocation, but compass-direction plus wind is routine description. Lithuanian damage to foliage, Serbian cold, and a helpful battlefield wind do not preserve a distinctive shared figure.

Three related lexical items and comparable travel setting, but green vegetation and riding through woodland are generic. Lithuanian reaches the forest whereas Serbian rides through it; no special narrative or formulaic constraint excludes independent composition.

Lithuanian remains of an animal contrast with Old Russian a moose trampling with feet and another goring with horns. Cognate material does not establish the same merism; the Russian coordination distinguishes two animals and two attacks.

Lithuanian Christian saint Margaret is called sister and holy; Avestan Ashi is sister OF the holy immortals, not holy modifying sister. Different attachment plus Christian context blocks the equation.
True ask/gold cognates, but ordinary transaction language: Lithuanian payment alternatives and Plautine offer of money. No distinctive inherited formula established.

The slab Indic partner concerns swallowing on the water’s back, not drinking sweet mead. Searches for sweet madhu find sweet food/ritual or comparative sweetness rather than the same mead-drinking phrase; Norse mead results have different adjectives. No defensible same-context partner for a search-lead record.

Lithuanian sadness and Serbian lud describing a seven-year-old sister are different senses, not a shared figure demonstrably bridging them. Repeated song-index entries are not independent attestations.

search_lead.cognate: Lithuanian aušra and aušti continue dawn/become-light material corresponding to Vedic uṣas and vas/uch. Slab auszra is aušrą, accusative singular; ausztancze is auštančią, feminine accusative singular active present participle agreeing with dawn.
search_lead.argument: Lithuanian the dawning dawn is an object with agreeing participle; Vedic Dawn has dawned and will dawn makes the same etymological figure with finite predicates. The redundant dawn + dawn collocation is a plausible inherited poetic figure, though productive cognate-word formation and the late Lithuanian song require caution. Cato, the supplied slab partner, has no such phrase, so this remains outside the anchored claims.
